newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton-Indian traders see dim hope for more export.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-Indian traders see dim hope for more export.

text.p: Firm Indian cotton prices have scotched hopes of further exports in the 1996/97 (October/September) season, traders said on Thursday.
"The government's philosophy is to help farmers get fair prices. When the prices are good, there is no need for further exports," said leading cotton trader Chandubhai Thakkar.
The government has already authorised exports of 1.2 million bales (170 kgs each) in the current season against 1.59 million bales in 1995/96.
Traders had been expecting authorisation of at least an additional 200,000 bales following last month's official estimate of the 1996/97 crop at 16 million bales, the same as in the previous year.
Thakkar said the government might consider allowing more exports of cotton yarn than raw cotton to meet the demand from mills.
"So I see a steady to firm trend in cotton prices during the rest of the season," he said.
In the week to Thursday, cotton prices settled 800-1,200 rupees higher per candy (355.56 kg), after rising steeply on hopes the government might allow higher cotton exports.
"While export hopes, coupled with reduced crop arrivals spurred speculative demand, sluggish mill demand and strigent monetary conditions neutralised their positive impact on prices," Thakkar said.

Arrivals of cotton dropped during the week due to end-season considerations. Daily average arrivals in the northern region of Punjab fell to 8,000/10,000 bales (170 kg each) against 15,000/20,000 bales reported last month.
Thakkar said nearly 12/12.50 million bales out of a total estimated crop of 16 million had arrived in the market.
"I am expecting arrivals to drop next month pushing prices further up," he said.
